summary: Defines an experimental method for providing multicast distribution-tree accounting data. Simple extensions to PIM give a rough approximation of tree-based information in a scalable way.

plainLanguage.summary: When one video goes to many viewers, nobody counts them. This experiment adds a rough way to estimate how many are on the delivery tree.

questions: how to count receivers in multicast
subtitle: A way for multicast routers to count receivers and characterize distribution trees.

tldr.problem: Multicast networks lack efficient ways to count active receivers or gather statistics about the distribution tree. Current approaches require correlating data from multiple routers, making it difficult to know how many hosts are receiving a given multicast stream or to characterize the tree's structure.
tldr.mechanism: Simple extensions to the PIM protocol allow routers to exchange accounting data in Join/Prune messages, including counts of receivers, tree diameter, bandwidth constraints, and domain crossings. The information is fixed-size and does not grow with tree size or membership changes.
tldr.outcome: The specification is experimental. Deployment and feedback across real multicast trees will help determine whether the mechanism should move to standards track, and what impact PIM accounting has on protocol stability.

today: RFC 6807 remains experimental. Deployment of this accounting mechanism in production networks has been limited. The specification is complete enough for implementation, but further reports of real-world use will inform whether it should move to standards track and what optimizations may be needed.

sections.title: Multicast Accounting and Distribution Tree Data
sections.content:
Multicast protocols like PIM deliver data from one or more sources to many receivers efficiently by building distribution trees. However, operators lack good visibility into tree properties and membership. To count receivers or track tree characteristics today, one must query multiple routers and correlate the data—a complex, fragmented process.

This specification defines a mechanism for routers to advertise accounting information using PIM's Join/Prune messages, which all routers on the tree exchange periodically. The data is efficient: the amount of information is fixed and does not grow as the tree expands, membership changes, or the tree branches more.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking many routers individually, accounting data travels with the PIM messages that routers already send. One number tells you about the whole sub-tree.

sections.title: Hello Option and Join Attribute Format
sections.content:
Routers announce support for this mechanism using a new PIM Hello option. When a router learns that its neighbor supports the feature, and when join attributes are enabled on the interface, the router includes a new Join Attribute in its Join/Prune messages.

The attribute carries an effective MTU (the minimum link MTU on the distribution tree), six flag bits (indicating membership type, tunnel presence, and complete sub-tree coverage), and an options bitmap. The bitmap indicates which of eight optional fields are present: transit and stub link counts, minimum and maximum link speeds, domain count, node count, tree diameter, and time-zone count. Each field is fixed-size, keeping the message overhead minimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers add a small label to their normal messages: 'here is the slowest link' or 'I count 5 receivers below me'. The label tells you which pieces of info are included.

sections.title: Counting and Measuring Tree Properties
sections.content:
The specification defines how each piece of accounting information is accumulated and propagated:

Link counts: Transit links (joined by PIM routers) and stub links (joined by hosts via IGMP or MLD) are counted separately. Each router sums its own links with counts received from downstream joiners.

Tree diameter: The longest path in hops from any router to a leaf. Each router increments the maximum diameter it receives from downstreams by one.

Node count: Total routers on the tree. Each router sums counts from downstreams and adds one for itself.

Link speeds: Minimum and maximum bandwidth rates are tracked using a compact two-octet encoding (exponent and significand) that represents speeds from 1 kbps to 10^67 kbps.

Domain and time-zone counts: Routers increment these when sending Join/Prune messages across domain or time-zone boundaries, using configured or other knowledge of link attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router adds up what it sees locally and what it hears from below. Slow links, far reaches, and zone boundaries all get noted. The result travels upstream with the join messages.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations can store accounting values per route or per interface, combining local information with data from downstream joiners when sending Join/Prune messages. When a downstream joiner leaves, implementations can either keep per-joiner records to adjust values when the joiner departs, or reset the affected oif and accumulate new values from subsequent joins.

Changes to accounting values do not trigger new Join/Prune messages; they are piggybacked on the periodic PIM schedule (typically once per minute). When triggered joins are sent for convergence speed, implementations should omit accounting data to minimize processing and message size.

This mechanism requires all routers on a distribution tree to support it for complete tree accounting. However, contiguous subtrees of supporting routers can still provide accounting for that portion of the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep track on their own and only send updates when they normally would. Fastest changes use plain PIM; accounting info tags along without slowing things down.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Future Considerations
sections.content:
This specification is experimental because the impact of PIM-based accounting on protocol stability and performance is not fully understood. It is a new concept in PIM; while other PIM extensions preceded their standardization in experimental form, this mechanism is fundamentally different in adding accounting responsibilities to a routing protocol.

The specification does not define how administrators or users access the collected information (such as through CLI or MIB). If the mechanism moves to standards track, a MIB module should be defined. Reports of successful deployment across entire distribution trees or within operational sub-trees will inform whether this work should advance and what safeguards or optimizations are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is new territory, so the engineers are calling it 'experimental' while they see if it works well and doesn't break anything.
